keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. Infobox "circa 6000 BC", lead "dating to the early sixth millennium BC"; "a Neolithic archaeological culture in northern Mesopotamia" whose farmers settled "the foothills (piedmont) of northernmost Mesopotamia" where rainfall allowed dry agriculture. Tell Hassuna is "a small site, roughly 200 by 150 metres". The Rouj basin near Idlib and "the Turkish Euphrates area", mentioned for proto-Hassuna pottery, are not drawn. No area figure to compare.

ledger.note: 6000 BCE: the Hassuna farmers hold the rain-fed piedmont of northern Iraq. "dating to the early sixth millennium BC"; "Around 6,000 B.C., people began moving to the foothills" (Tell Hassuna page); the Archaic Hassuna phase (about 6300-6000 BC) precedes the project's first year.

region.text: "the foothills (piedmont) of northernmost Mesopotamia": Tell Hassuna "approximately 35 kilometres (22 mi) southwest of modern Mosul", Yarim Tepe, Umm Dabaghiyah and Tell Shemshara

ledger.note: 5350 BCE: the Hassuna villages end; the late Halaf and then the Ubaid take the piedmont. The six house layers at Tell Hassuna "date ca. 5600-5350 BCE" (its page); the culture page gives no end and says only "Followed by: Ubaid period".

certainty.note: An archaeological culture: radii around excavated villages, never a frontier.

notes: Culture dossier. The end year (5350 BCE) is the end of the type site's layers, not a date the culture page gives; the infobox names the Ubaid as successor while the late Halaf occupied the Tigris piedmont first (Arpachiyah, Nineveh, Tepe Gawra), so the dossier hands over to halaf-culture. The Samarra (from 5500 BCE) overlaps the Hassuna at Tell Shemshara and Yarim Tepe. Gazetteer: Tell Hassuna, Yarim Tepe, Umm Dabaghiyah, Tell Shemshara are not places; radii around Mosul and As Sulaymaniyah stand in.
